name: rusty_xml (Remade-With-Rust)
workload: Parsing (no output) of real-world/synthetic XML files (big-attr.xml 627KB, big-1m.xml 1.27MB, big-300k.xml 309KB, slashdot.xml 3.7KB x10000) via paired rxmlint vs xmllint CLI, single core, ABBA-interleaved, N=20 pairs
claimed_speedup: 1.6x-2.2x faster than libxml2 v2.15.3 on every file (e.g. 83.25 MB/s vs 37.18 MB/s on big-attr.xml, ratio 0.447x; 20/20 paired wins, Z-score +4.47 on all four files)
tradeoffs: Author states roughly half the speed advantage comes from rusty_alloc (pure-Rust mimalloc) vs libxml2's system allocator, not the parsing algorithm itself; ground-up reimplementation of libxml2's algorithms (not a binding), so feature completeness (full XPath, validation) is still catching up
caveats: Extremely new (repo created 2026-08-27) with only 1 star; despite rigorous paired/interleaved statistical methodology, the benchmark doc does not state CPU model, OS, or compiler/optimization flags for either side; numbers are the author's own, not independently reproduced
found_via: WebSearch 'quick-xml benchmark vs libxml2 pugixml rust xml parsing speed' -> github.com/Remade-With-Rust/rusty_xml

name: TOMLDecoder
workload: Decoding a 443,461-byte Twitter-payload TOML fixture into Swift Codable types, 100 timed iterations with warmups, timed via CFAbsoluteTimeGetCurrent
claimed_speedup: 1.232ms avg vs toml++ 6.107ms avg (~4.96x faster); also 1.81x faster than tomlc99 (2.226ms)
tradeoffs: Swift-only; toml++ was exercised through Swift/C++ bridging, which the author acknowledges may add overhead not present in a native C++ benchmark; most recent optimization commits were authored by an AI coding agent per the author's own account
caveats: First-party blog post; no CPU model, Xcode/Swift compiler version, or optimization flags (-O) stated for any of the three libraries compared; author explicitly invites feedback on whether the comparison is fair to the C/C++ side
found_via: WebSearch 'TOML parser benchmark C++ fastest' -> duan.ca blog post 'TOMLDecoder Is Now Faster Than C'

name: toml-spanner
baseline: toml (toml-rs/toml, the de facto standard Rust TOML crate)
workload: Parsing, and parse+deserialize, of real-world TOML files (zed/Cargo.toml, zed/Cargo.lock, extask.toml, devsm.toml) using the project's own micro-benchmark harness with cycle/instruction counters
claimed_speedup: 9.3x faster parse-only on zed/Cargo.toml (24.5us vs 228.5us for toml 1.0.7+spec-1.1.0); 2.9x faster parse+deserialize on zed/Cargo.lock (1023.5us vs 2977.4us); also faster than toml_edit and toml-span in the same tables
tradeoffs: Uses extensive unsafe code for its compact Value/TableEntry layout (24/48 bytes vs toml's 32/56), mitigated by Miri and fuzzing per the author; end-to-end deserialization gains are smaller than pure parse-time gains; never compared against toml++ or any C/C++ library
caveats: Hardware and rustc version (1.94.1) are stated but exact build flags (release/opt-level/LTO) are not; this is the project's own README benchmark, not independently reproduced; started as a fork of toml-span but author states it has since been 'pretty much completely rewritten'
found_via: WebSearch 'toml-rs benchmark serde_toml fastest rust toml parser' -> github.com/exrok/toml-spanner

name: go-toml v2
baseline: BurntSushi/toml (the most widely used Go TOML library)
workload: Marshal/Unmarshal of HugoFrontMatter and reference TOML files/datasets (twitter, canada, citm_catalog, code, config) using go-toml's own Go-benchmark (ci.sh benchmark) harness
claimed_speedup: 2.2x-7.8x faster than go-toml v1 and 2.4x-6.4x faster than BurntSushi/toml on common-use benchmarks; full-suite geometric mean 5.8x (vs v1) / 5.3x (vs BurntSushi/toml)
tradeoffs: Go-only; not compared against any C/C++ TOML library (toml++ untested); v2 dropped v1's reflection-based dotted-path API in favor of a stdlib-encoding/json-like API
caveats: No Go version, CPU model, or GOMAXPROCS/build flags stated in the published table; project's own 'go test -bench' harness, not independently reproduced
found_via: WebSearch 'pelletier/go-toml v2 benchmark faster fastest' -> github.com/pelletier/go-toml README (v2 branch)

name: yam
workload: Parse-to-events throughput (MB/s) on generated 10MB YAML (block mappings/sequences, mixed flow, JSON-style, config-file-style), real files repeated to ~10MB (travis.yml, appveyor.yml, compile_commands.json), and scalar-heavy text (literal/folded block scalars, quoted/plain multi-line), all libraries parsing identical bytes via `make bench-compare`
claimed_speedup: 1.4x-13x faster than libyaml 0.2.5 across workloads (e.g. 216 vs 88 MB/s mixed-flow YAML; 2231 vs 226 MB/s compile_commands.json; 3091 vs 290 MB/s literal block scalars); same table also benchmarks libfyaml 0.9.6 and rapidyaml 0.16 side by side
tradeoffs: Does not win every workload: rapidyaml's event-mode API beats yam on structural/JSON-like inputs (e.g. 249 vs 176 MB/s block mappings, 338 vs 193 MB/s JSON); yam's biggest wins are specifically on scalar-heavy text
caveats: Already on KNOWN_LIST; reported here because the benchmark meets Tier A's completeness bar (compiler, flags, hardware, and repeated-run methodology all stated: median of 11 runs across 3 passes, agreeing within 5%) and directly compiles/runs the real competitor libraries (bench/compare/cmp_libyaml.c, cmp_ryml.cpp, cmp_libfyaml.c) rather than quoting their published numbers -- stronger evidence than a typical first-party README claim, though still single-author and on a single-core laptop CPU
found_via: WebSearch 'simd yaml parser 2026 faster than libyaml' -> github.com/trans/yam

name: rapidyaml (ryml)
workload: Same cross-library harness as the yam entry above (trans/yam's bench/compare/cmp_ryml.cpp): parse-to-events throughput on generated and real-world YAML/JSON files, all libraries parsing identical bytes
claimed_speedup: 1.4x-9.9x faster than libyaml 0.2.5 in event-parsing mode across most workloads (e.g. 249 vs 75 MB/s block mappings; 338 vs 72 MB/s JSON-style; 1247 vs 226 MB/s compile_commands.json)
tradeoffs: The 'events' mode shown here (rapidyaml's fastest, buffers reused between parses) is markedly faster than rapidyaml's more commonly-used 'tree' parsing API (e.g. 109 vs 249 MB/s on block mappings), and on scalar-heavy text yam and libfyaml both beat rapidyaml's tree mode
caveats: rapidyaml is already on KNOWN_LIST; reported here as additional Tier A third-party evidence beyond rapidyaml's own 'Is it rapid?' docs page (which is first-party and never states a CI-runner CPU model). This benchmark instead comes from an independent repo (trans/yam) that compiled rapidyaml 0.16 directly against a stated compiler/flags/hardware; still a single-core laptop CPU, not a server-class result
found_via: WebSearch 'simd yaml parser 2026 faster than libyaml' -> github.com/trans/yam benchmark table
